rows.evidence: Q1: Materials and Methods (Modeling Framework, Solving the Model) and Results, Table 2 <U+2013> authors run their own basin-scale hydroeconomic optimization model of the Upper Rio Grande Basin for drip-subsidy scenarios from 0 to 100% capital subsidy, reporting annual-average hydrologic outcomes 2006-2025.
rows.notes: The study's own result matches the claim in substance: Table 2 shows that as drip subsidy rises, aquifer storage gains fall from 74,000 to 40,000 acre-feet/yr and aquifer-to-river gains fall from 32,000 to 17,000, because drip is assumed to produce zero deep percolation (Table 1). However, this is an optimization-model output, not a measured result; the only check against observations is that the base-case technology shares (~90% flood, <10% drip) 'correspond approximately' to actual 2006 EBID conditions, and the recharge/return-flow outputs themselves are never compared with measurements. Crop-level water applied, ET and deep percolation inputs are typical design values. Under the rule that a model run on design data or not checked against observations is 'no', Q2 is answered 'no'; this is a judgement call and the model is otherwise fully basin-scale. Study also notes (footnote **) that where return flows go to saline sinks, reduced applications do save water.

rows.evidence: Q1: Materials and Methods and Results, Tables 2-3 <U+2013> authors' own basin-scale hydroeconomic optimization model runs of drip-irrigation subsidy scenarios for the Rio Grande Basin.
rows.notes: Model results (Tables 2-3) show a rebound-type outcome: higher drip subsidies reduce water applied (364,000 to 324,000 af/yr) but raise ET (167,000 to 204,000), total irrigated acreage (75,000 to 87,000 acres), yields and farm income, giving negative conservation of ~36,700 af/yr at 100% subsidy. This is consistent with the passage. But the result is a simulated optimization output on design-type crop data; model outputs on depletion and acreage are not compared with measurements from the real system (only base-case technology shares are loosely said to match 2006 EBID conditions). Hence Q2 'no' under the model-validation rule. Note also the model does not represent reallocation of savings to competing users; it shows expansion and intensification within the district.

rows.evidence: Q1: Materials and Methods and Results, Tables 2-3 <U+2013> authors' own dynamic nonlinear optimization model of the basin run for 11 drip-subsidy levels.
rows.notes: The study's modeled result matches the passage: water applied falls under drip subsidies while irrigated land expands (75,000 to 87,000 acres), drip acreage rises to 53% of land, and basin-level consumptive use (ET) increases; depletion never falls below base level. However, the study's own Table 1 shows per-acre water consumption (ET) is higher under drip, so the 'reduction in water consumption' part of the passage is not what the model shows <U+2013> only water applied declines. More importantly, the effect is a simulation output not checked against observed depletion or acreage data (only a loose statement that base-case technology shares approximate actual 2006 conditions), so Q2 is 'no' per the model rule.

rows.evidence: Q1: Materials and Methods and Results, Table 2 <U+2013> authors' own basin-scale hydroeconomic model runs.
rows.notes: The study models the hydrologic redistribution (Table 2: aquifer-to-river gains fall 32,000 to 17,000 af/yr, downstream delivery falls 314,000 to 292,000 af/yr under high drip subsidy) but does not model or measure impacts on existing water right holders, equity or social cohesion. The statement that reduced return flows 'could impair existing water right holders' appears only in the Conclusions as an inference. The study therefore supports at most a precondition (altered return flows/downstream supply) of the claimed social effect, and that precondition is itself an unvalidated model output. Q2 'no', upstream true.

rows.evidence: Q1: Materials and Methods and Results, Table 2 <U+2013> authors' own basin-scale optimization model runs for drip-subsidy scenarios.
rows.notes: The study's model shows return flows and aquifer recharge fall and downstream delivery declines with drip adoption (Table 2), which corresponds to 'reduced availability for other uses'; but 'complicating water governance' is only discussed in the Conclusions (water rights should be defined in depletions; effects hard to measure and delayed), not analysed as a result. The function rated is social_cohesion/governance, for which the study offers argument, not evidence. The hydrologic precondition is a model output not compared with observations. Q2 'no', upstream true.

notes: The study is a basin-scale hydroeconomic optimization model (Upper Rio Grande / Elephant Butte Irrigation District) run for drip-subsidy scenarios 0-100% over 2006-2025; it reports its own model runs (Q1 yes) but no field measurements. The only comparison with the real system is a statement that the base-case flood/drip shares approximate actual 2006 EBID conditions; the hydrologic outputs (ET, recharge, return flow, depletion) that underlie all claims are not validated against observations and rest on typical crop-level inputs (e.g., drip deep percolation assumed 0). Under the instruction that unvalidated or design-data model runs do not count as own evidence, Q2 is 'no' for all rows; a less strict reader might accept the basin-scale model as evidence for rows 1-3, in which case Q6 (basin/district scale) and Q7 (effect requires return flows to be recoverable, not lost to saline sinks <U+2013> footnote **) would plausibly be 'yes', while Q3, Q4 (ET and return flows are tracked by mass balance), Q5, Q8 and Q9 would largely remain 'no' (no dispersion or uncertainty analysis reported; limitations stated only in footnotes about excluded environmental values). Supporting information (Figs. S1-S2) is not included in the text supplied.
